items.title: Arrive Tottori — dunes at golden hour
items.pace: Arrival day: settle in, then the Sand Dunes and Sand Museum in the afternoon/evening.
items.tldr: Land, drop bags, and spend the afternoon at the free Sand Dunes and the paid Sand Museum next door.
items.body:
However you route in (see the Plan tab — no flight is confirmed yet), get to Tottori Station and check into the city for one night before the group splits its luggage load toward Kurayoshi and Misasa tomorrow.

The Tottori Sand Dunes are free to enter with free dune-side parking — no ticket, no gate, just go. Next door, the Sand Museum (¥800, 9:00–18:00, last entry 17:30) is running its Spain-themed 17th exhibition through Jan 2027, so it'll be the Spain sculptures on display for this visit. Between the two, this is an easy, low-effort first afternoon that doesn't ask much of anyone's legs.

One trade to make knowingly: the dunes' quiet window is dawn, not late afternoon (see the Sights tab), and this plan spends the afternoon slot instead. Wednesday morning, before the castle ruins, is the only dawn slot the four days contain — worth it for whoever wants the photographs, not worth waking the whole party for.

items.title: Tottori Castle ruins, then the transfer day: Kurayoshi and the last bus to Misasa
items.pace: Morning at Kyusho Park/castle ruins in Tottori, midday train to Kurayoshi, afternoon in the Shirakabe warehouse district, wagyu dinner, then the 19:25 bus to Misasa.
items.tldr: The whole day builds toward one bus: dinner in Kurayoshi has to end in time for the last practical departure to Misasa Onsen.
items.body:
Start at Tottori Castle ruins in Kyusho Park — free, outdoor, an easy morning walk. Jinpukaku, the Meiji-era Western mansion on the same grounds, is under renovation-closure through roughly 2028 and its exterior is currently sheeted, but the Horyu-in garden and Hosen-an teahouse beside it are still open.

Take the San'in Main Line to Kurayoshi (≈30 min limited express, ≈60 min local) and spend the afternoon in the Shirakabe Dozo-gun white-walled warehouse district — free to wander, with a tourist information center at Akagawara Building No. 10.

Lunch is the one slot Menya Hachibee fits into on this trip — it's minutes from Kurayoshi Station and its gyukotsu ramen is the local specialty. ⚠ Its hours aren't confirmed against a primary source and its reported lunch service ends early, so take the earlier train if the group wants it, and split across two sittings (see the Food tab).

Have dinner at Yakiniku Masashige (book ahead by phone for 8 — see the Food tab), aiming to be done well before 19:25, the last weekday Hinomaru Bus departure from Kurayoshi Station toward Misasa Onsen. This is the trip's anchor transfer: missing it means either an expensive multi-taxi scramble or an unplanned night in Kurayoshi.

The luggage is what this day breaks on if you improvise it. Eight people can't carry bags around a warehouse district and a yakiniku dinner, and the bus has no luggage hold.

If your ryokan runs the reserved shuttle (fixed afternoon pickups from Kurayoshi Station — see the Transit tab), that's the lever: send the bags, and the two travelers with low walking tolerance, over to Misasa on an afternoon run. The rest of the group does the district and dinner unencumbered and catches the 19:25. ⚠ Confirm at booking that the ryokan will carry luggage and passengers on separate runs.

plan_b.body: If the group runs late and the 19:25 bus is missed, reserve a 9-seat Hinomaru Hire jumbo taxi (0858-22-3155) rather than waiting for a next-day bus — one vehicle for the whole party of 8 with luggage, ≈20 minutes, at published metered rates (¥740 flagfall + ¥90/279m). It needs advance booking, not a station hail. If your ryokan runs its own free reserved shuttle, confirm that option when you book the room. Nikko/Chuo Taxi (0858-22-7111) or Kurayoshi Kotsu (0858-22-1511) are walk-up backups but likely need 2 cars for 8 people, and the only fare figure found for them dates to 2009.

items.title: Misasa Onsen — Nageiredo, the onsen town, and crab
items.pace: Early start for the mountain (fit members climb, others use the viewing platform), midday at Kabuyu, slow afternoon, crab dinner.
items.tldr: The National Treasure at Sanbutsu-ji splits the group by ability — a real climb for some, a free accessible viewpoint for everyone else — before the day settles into the onsen town.
items.body:
Sanbutsu-ji's Nageiredo — a National Treasure hall wedged into a cliff face — is the region's signature culture stop, and it's genuinely two different experiences depending on mobility. The climb itself (reception 8:00–15:00, mandatory 16:30 descent) requires a minimum of two people, hiking-style footwear, and is called off outright in rain or unsafe conditions (¥1,200 adult). For anyone who shouldn't attempt it, the free Nageiredo Yohaijo viewing platform gives a telescope view of the same hall without the climb, rain or shine; pair it with the ¥400 main-hall (hondo) visit, which also doesn't require the climb.

Getting up there without a car is a fixed-schedule problem, not a taxi decision. The 70/71 bus runs from the Misasa Onsen bus centre to the Mitokusan stop in about fifteen minutes, a handful of times a day, and the last return is late afternoon — pick the bus you're coming back on before anyone starts climbing. Times are in the Transit tab.

Midday, Kabuyu — Misasa Onsen's original source bath — is open through the afternoon (¥400 adult) with a free footbath and drinking-spring station alongside it. Leave the rest of the afternoon unscheduled; this is the trip's slow day.

Crab is the evening's theme, but not the one Tottori is famous for: matsuba-gani is a November–March catch and isn't landed during this trip. Beni-zuwaigani (red snow crab) runs September–June and is in season through the visit — ask for it by name at your ryokan's dinner.

plan_b.body: If weather closes Nageiredo for the day, the group isn't shut out of the site: the Yohaijo viewing platform stays open regardless of weather, and the ¥400 Sanbutsu-ji main hall visit is unaffected. Shift the freed-up time to an earlier, longer Kabuyu/footbath session instead.

items.title: Departure — back to Kurayoshi and onward
items.pace: Slow morning in Misasa, mid-morning bus back to Kurayoshi Station, onward travel.
items.tldr: One more soak, then the same bus route in reverse — mornings run more often than the evening service you relied on Day 2.
items.body:
A last footbath or onsen dip before checkout. Morning Hinomaru Bus service from Misasa back toward Kurayoshi Station is denser than the evening run the group used on Day 2 — departures from the Misasa Onsen bus centre start before 7:40 — which gives more slack for a final-day transfer with luggage than the outbound leg had.

From Kurayoshi Station, connect onward by San'in Line limited express toward Okayama/Shin-Osaka for Shinkansen connections, or toward Tottori Airport if that ends up being the confirmed routing.

title: Health & pharmacy
body:
Emergency numbers: 110 for police, 119 for fire or ambulance. The JNTO Japan Visitor Hotline (050-3816-2787, also reachable from overseas) runs 24/7 in English, Chinese, Korean, and Japanese, and explicitly covers emergency support for illness and disasters — not just tourist questions. If you're unsure whether a situation needs an ambulance, #7119 is a nurse-staffed triage line.

⚠ This itinerary spends most of two days in Kurayoshi and Misasa Onsen, both smaller towns than Tottori city — pharmacy and clinic density there is lower, and it's worth locating your ryokan's nearest clinic on arrival rather than assuming Tottori-city coverage extends out to Misasa.

title: Etiquette & language
body:
Shoes come off at ryokan entrances, temple interiors, and some restaurants with tatami seating — Kurayoshi's old-town eateries and any Misasa Onsen ryokan both apply. Wash and rinse fully at the shower stalls before getting into a shared bath at Kabuyu or a ryokan's onsen; swimwear isn't worn in the water.

⚠ Tattoo policy varies by venue, and Kabuyu's exact policy — along with any specific Misasa ryokan's — couldn't be confirmed here. Japan's tourism agency has told operators that a blanket tattoo ban isn't appropriate, but many onsen still enforce one. If anyone in the party has visible tattoos, ask directly (or look for a private-bath option) before assuming access.

English signage thins out once you're past Tottori Station, and this guide has no phrase card. ⚠ Save the stop names you'll actually need in a form you can show a driver or a bus driver: 倉吉駅 (Kurayoshi Station), 三朝温泉観光商工センター前 (Misasa Onsen bus centre), 三徳山駐車場 (Mitokusan, for Sanbutsu-ji).
